claim: MTDSim is an existing MTD simulator.
quote: This paper proposes an evaluation framework named MTDSim, which is a simulation-based tool to evaluate the effectiveness of combinations of MTD techniques

claim: MTDSim simulates an attacker and MTD on one network.
quote: We develop an MTD evaluation framework named MTDSim, which will be used to simulate the system, attacker, and defense.
issue: Brown also runs both scenarios 'in identical networks' (§III-C), so 'one network' holds.

claim: MTDSim evaluates MTD mechanisms singly and in combination.
quote: When a single MTD was used, the host shuffle performed the best, followed by port shuffling. The trend continued in double MTD

claim: Each deeper level is a set of subnets of hosts.
quote: the graphs are generated using the Barabasi-Albert graph model [16] to generate small subnets in each level of depth

claim: The subnets are small groups of densely linked hosts, joined to the level before it, so reaching a level requires a compromised host in the level before it.
quote: Internal hosts will also be displayed if they are able to establish a path through a compromised or exposed internal host.
issue: Brown says only that subnets are small and Barabasi-Albert generated; 'densely linked', the joining of each level to the one before, and the level-by-level reachability rule are not in Brown's text (Fig. 2 is an image, not in the text cache); Brown's rule is a path through any compromised or exposed host.
fix_text: 'small groups of densely linked hosts' -> 'small groups of hosts'; cite tay2024code for the level-to-level joining if it is the generator's rule

claim: Each vulnerability has an attack complexity from CVSS, and an impact.
quote: Vulnerabilities are generated with an attack complexity and impact, derived from the CVSS scoring system [23].

claim: Attack complexity sets the probability that an exploit succeeds; impact is the damage a successful exploit does.
quote: The attack complexity would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0.4, 1] and the impact decides the reward for compromising the vulnerability
issue: Brown says complexity decides the 'difficulty' of exploiting and impact the attacker's 'reward'; neither 'probability that an exploit succeeds' nor 'damage' is Brown's (the probability reading is the code's).
fix_text: 'which sets the probability that an exploit succeeds' -> 'which sets how hard it is to exploit'; 'the damage a successful exploit does' -> 'the reward for exploiting it'

claim: The MTD mechanisms come from Brown's pool, added to by Zhang (Brown supplies six of the seven).
quote: The following MTD techniques are implemented for evaluations, which cover various types of MTD techniques in multiple system layers.
issue: Brown's §III-B lists IP shuffle, port shuffle, user access shuffle, host topology shuffle, service diversity and OS diversity: six of the seven, complete topology shuffle being Zhang's.

claim: The table's grouping and cells describe the mechanisms of Brown's pool (cells say each acts on 'every internal host').
quote: In MTDSim, this was implemented by randomly changing the OS on each host, which also randomly changed services on the host that were incompatible with the new OS.
locator: p. 4 printed (PDF p. 4), §III-B(6); also §III-B(2) 'all exposed services', §III-B(3) 'on each host'
issue: The caption's credit to Brown sits over cells that restrict OS diversity, service diversity, port shuffle and user shuffle to internal hosts; Brown restricts only IP shuffle to 'internal hosts' and applies the others to each host (port shuffle: 'all exposed services'). The exemption is this repo's D-23 (beyond-paper). The neighbour U0077 ('no MTD mechanism changes them') states the same departure uncited.
fix_text: keep the caption; if the endpoint exemption should read as ours, add to U0077 'in the released code' or similar

claim: The baseline attacker is the attacker MTDSim was built with.
quote: The Attacker is modeled as a theoretically intelligent adversary, which will follow a logical flowchart inspired by the Cyber Kill Chain [17] and MITRE ATT&CK Framework [18].

claim: The attacker follows a fixed procedure.
quote: All attacker agents in the simulation will always follow the attack procedure (as shown in Figure 3) to decide their next move.

claim: The procedure is modelled on the Cyber Kill Chain.
quote: The adversaries are implemented to follow a process similar to the Cyber Kill Chain [17] and MITRE ATT&CK Framework [18] as depicted in Figure 3.
issue: Brown attributes the procedure to the Cyber Kill Chain and ATT&CK jointly, and lists both as a contribution (§I); the sentence keeps only the kill chain (cut deliberately per the tex comment), which undersells the predecessor in a dissertation whose contribution is ATT&CK-derived behaviour. The supervisor co-authored the claim.
fix_text: 'modelled on the Cyber Kill Chain' -> 'modelled on the Cyber Kill Chain and ATT&CK' (ATT&CK is cited in 3.1.2; a forward reference or the cite here)

claim: The procedure is six attack actions: scan hosts, enumerate one, scan ports, exploit, brute force, scan neighbours of each compromised host.
quote: The attacker will commence with the host discovery phase. This encompasses performing a scan on the network to discover all exposed hosts. Internal hosts will also be displayed if they are able to establish a path through a compromised or exposed internal host. Host reconnaissance is performed next, running port scans to discover exposed services or internal services that are connected to the compromised service. The attacker will first attempt to perform a credentialstuffing attack using user account information from previously compromised hosts.
issue: Brown's prose names host discovery, port scan, credential stuffing, exploitation, command and control and brute force; it never counts six actions or names 'enumerate'. The six-verb list (Scan Host, Enum Host, ..., Scan Neighbour) is Zhang's Fig. 7 and the code; Brown's Fig. 3 ('Pick a Target Host from Priority Stack', per the intent-spec transcription) is an image not in the text cache, so this could not be quoted.
fix_text: '[brown2023, hutchins2011]' -> '[brown2023, zhang2023, hutchins2011]', or move zhang2023 onto the six-verb list

claim: MTDSim's attacker has two attack scenarios, defined by goal: general (as many hosts as possible) and targeted (a target host).
quote: MTDSim looks to address this by implementing two attack scenarios with the same capabilities but with different goals in identical networks
issue: Goals per §III-C(1): 'attempting to compromise the whole network' and 'compromise a specific ”target” host'.

claim: On each host it tries stolen credentials first, then exploits vulnerabilities in RoA order, and brute force last.
quote: The attacker will first attempt to perform a credentialstuffing attack using user account information from previously compromised hosts. Next, a service from the scanning will be selected for exploitation. The vulnerabilities from all the services scanned will be put into a priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA) [13].
issue: Brute force last: 'If the attack fails, they will then commence a brute force attack.' (same paragraph).

claim: Return on attack is an exploit's probability of success times its impact, divided by the time it takes.
quote: The vulnerabilities from all the services scanned will be put into a priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA) [13].
issue: Brown gives no RoA formula; it borrows RoA from its ref. [13] (Alavizadeh et al. 2018). The time-as-cost form is Ho's / the code's (services.py, intent spec IS-MET-04). The cite sits directly after the definition, so the definition reads as Brown's.
fix_text: move '\citep{brown2023}' to after 'in order of \emph{return on attack}'; source the definition 'probability of success times its impact, divided by the time it takes' to tay2024code (or ho2024), with alavizadeh2022 for RoA itself

claim: It gives up on a host after ten attempts, but never on a target host.
quote: the attacker agent will move on after trying to exploit for 10 times without being able to compromise the host currently selected. However, when the attacker is conducting a targeted attack (i.e., scenario 2), the attacker is set to never give up on the target node.
locator: p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7), §V-C; Table I p. 5

claim: A vulnerability's attack complexity lies between 0.4 and 1.
quote: The attack complexity would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0.4, 1]
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), §III-A; Table I p. 5

claim: An exploit takes 15 s times one minus the attack complexity (0 to 9 s).
quote: Vulnerabilities are generated with an attack complexity and impact, derived from the CVSS scoring system [23].
issue: Brown gives no exploit duration; the 15 s formula is the code's (tex comment: services.py Vulnerability.exploit_time). The only cite in the sentence is [brown2023], so the formula can read as Brown's. Outside Brown: the tex comment says the x2.5 OS-mismatch factor is left off, so '0 to 9 s' is not the full range in the code.
fix_text: 'times one minus the vulnerability's attack complexity' -> add '\citep{tay2024code}' after 'attack complexity'

claim: A service-layer deployment sends the attacker back to scanning the same host's ports.
quote: Service and Operating System Diversity, and Port Shuffle all change the services on the host. This would either change the ports that the services are run on or change the service itself, changing the vulnerabilities. This would block the attacker from compromising the vulnerability and force them to re-perform a port scan to understand the new service or the service location.
issue: Brown's service class is exactly Table 2.3's service layer (OS diversity, service diversity, port shuffle).

claim: A service-layer deployment disrupts the attacker only while it scans ports, exploits or brute-forces.
quote: This would block the attacker from compromising the vulnerability and force them to re-perform a port scan
issue: Brown says the service class blocks the attacker from compromising the vulnerability, i.e. the exploit; the 'only while it scans ports, exploits or brute-forces' window is Zhang's application-layer enclosure (Fig. 7) and the code, not Brown.

claim: (Uncited neighbour, leans on Brown.) A host-layer deployment disrupts the attacker during any attack action and sends it back to scanning hosts, because the host it was on may have moved.
quote: IP Shuffle and Host Topology Shuffle change the location of the host by changing the IP or the host itself. This would result in the attacker’s connection to the host being terminated or timed out. As they would be uncertain of the status of the hosts, they would be forced to re-perform the host discovery phase to find new paths to the hosts.
issue: The re-scan and its reason are Brown's and uncited here; 'during any attack action' is Zhang's network-layer enclosure (Fig. 7), not Brown.

claim: (Uncited neighbour, leans on Brown.) A user shuffle disrupts only brute force, and sends it to exploit instead.
quote: When User Shuffle is performed, the users on the host change. This would only block the attack if the attacker was performing a credential stuffing attack as the users are shuffled, forcing them to look for vulnerabilities on the host.
issue: Brown has a user shuffle block only credential stuffing (the first try, with stolen credentials), sending the attacker on to exploit; the sentence says brute force (the last try). It sits between two Brown-cited sentences, and the conformance audit labels the code's brute-force gate 'Brown's narrow blocking condition', which it is not. Since U0815 says behaviour was repaired where it departs from the prior studies, the supervisor would read this as either a misdescription or an unrepaired departure.
fix_text: 'A user shuffle disrupts only brute force' -> 'In the code, a user shuffle disrupts only brute force (Brown has it disrupt credential stuffing \citep{brown2023})', or repair the code to Brown's rule

claim: Brown's column: 200 hosts, 5 levels of depth, 20 subnets, 20 exposed endpoints, general and targeted scenarios, no stated run count.
quote: Total No. of Hosts 200 No. of exposed hosts 20 No. of layers 5 No. of subnets 20
issue: Brown's 'layers' are levels of depth (§III-A 'levels of depth'); no trial count anywhere ('similar between trials' only).

claim: Brown's deployment interval is uniform on 1-5 s.
quote: The MTDSim ran the simulation using a U nif orm(1000, 5000) (i.e., the Defense trigger time from the table), where E(T ) = 3000 (time in milliseconds).
issue: Conversion from ms is correct; Brown calls it the 'Defense trigger time'.

claim: Brown's end of run: whole network compromised; target host compromised.
quote: the attacker is looking to obtain the most amount of control by attempting to compromise the whole network.
issue: Brown states each scenario's goal, not when a run ends; the general attacker gives up on hosts after 10 attempts (§V-C), so it need not reach the whole network. 'End of run' turns a goal into a stopping rule Brown never states.
fix_text: 'whole network compromised; target host compromised' -> 'not stated (goal: the whole network; a target host)' or keep with the table's locator note saying 'the goal, read as the end of run'

claim: Attack actions blocked is a defender-side MTD effectiveness metric used by Brown.
quote: Finally, we evaluate the total actions blocked and also the average attempts required to compromise to evaluate the MTD techniques and their combinations.

claim: MTDSim's baseline attacker is a 2023 MTD attacker model, as described in Section 2.2.3.
quote: We implement realistic attack scenarios using Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK Framework;

claim: Baseline attacker row (2023): Pers. has; Obj. none; Strat. part; Adapt. part; Detect., Cost, Learn., Deploy. none.
quote: MTDSim looks to address this by implementing two attack scenarios with the same capabilities but with different goals in identical networks
issue: The marks are this dissertation's judgement and none contradicts Brown. Exposure: Cost 'none' while Brown orders vulnerabilities in a 'priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA)', the metric the dissertation itself lists as an efficiency measure; the supervisor may read that as cost-benefit reasoning (the tex comment of round 51 still records Cost as P, now stale).

claim: The baseline attacker repeats its attack actions host by host until it reaches its goal, and carries on through every disruption.
quote: MTDSim looks to counteract this by giving a time penalty whenever the attacker is blocked due to an MTD and forces them to re-scan the network to decide their next decision.
locator: p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7), §V-A; also §III-D, §V-C 'never give up on the target node'
issue: 'Six attack actions' is the dissertation's (Zhang's) count, not Brown's (see U0108).

claim: A fixed rule sets its response to each kind of disruption, such as always re-scanning after a host-layer disruption.
quote: As they would be uncertain of the status of the hosts, they would be forced to re-perform the host discovery phase to find new paths to the hosts.

claim: Brown describes scan neighbours as Command and Control revealing connected hosts.
quote: Once the attacker has successfully compromised a host, they will assume command and control functionality, making it possible to view internal services and hosts that are connected to it.
issue: Brown's prose calls the step C2 functionality, not 'scan neighbours'; the link to the attack action rests on Fig. 3 ('Scan for Neighbors to the Recently Compromised Host', per the intent-spec transcription), an image the quote check cannot verify.

claim: Attack actions blocked per MTD deployment is Brown's metric.
quote: Finally, we evaluate the total actions blocked and also the average attempts required to compromise to evaluate the MTD techniques and their combinations.
locator: p. 5 printed (PDF p. 5), §IV; Fig. 4 'Total actions blocked'
issue: Brown reports a total; dividing by the number of deployments is this dissertation's. Credited bare, unlike the neighbouring 'this dissertation, after [royston2013]' row. The supervisor will know his metric was a total.

claim: Attack actions blocked per MTD deployment = attack actions disrupted / MTD deployments, counted over every run, is Brown's.
quote: Finally, we evaluate the total actions blocked and also the average attempts required to compromise to evaluate the MTD techniques and their combinations.
issue: Brown counts total actions blocked, with no per-deployment normalisation; the cite sits after the division, so the ratio reads as Brown's. The tex comment shows the sentence saying Brown counts a total was cut.
fix_text: 'counting over every run \citep{brown2023}' -> 'counting over every run, after the total of Brown et al. \citep{brown2023}'

claim: The baseline attacker is Brown's.
quote: The Attacker is modeled as a theoretically intelligent adversary, which will follow a logical flowchart inspired by the Cyber Kill Chain [17] and MITRE ATT&CK Framework [18].

claim: The single deployment strategy over each of the seven mechanisms draws on Brown (six mechanisms, single MTD) and Zhang.
quote: When a single MTD was used, the host shuffle performed the best, followed by port shuffling.
locator: p. 5 printed (PDF p. 5), §IV-A; §III-B for the six

claim: The targeted attack scenario is Brown's.
quote: In the Target Attack Scenario, like APT-style attacks, the attacker is looking to compromise a specific ”target” host (e.g., a credential database).

claim: A run ends when a target host is compromised, per Brown.
